pos: n. (the eleventh son of Ishmael, head of one of the twelve Ishmaelite princes)
etymology: Hebrew Naphish, refreshment, or breathing, from naphash, to take breath or be refreshed; named at Genesis 25:15 and 1 Chronicles 1:31.
biblical_def: Naphish is one of the twelve sons of Ishmael: “Hadar, and Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah” (Genesis 25:15), repeated in the Chronicler's roll, “Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael” (1 Chronicles 1:31). The verse that follows in Genesis explains what the list is: “These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their towns, and by their castles; twelve princes according to their nations” (Genesis 25:16). Twelve princes — the number is not accidental. God had promised Abraham concerning Ishmael, I will make him a great nation, and twelve princes shall he beget, and Genesis 25 records the promise kept, name by name, in the same chapter that records Abraham's death. Naphish reappears centuries later as a tribe: the Reubenites, Gadites and half Manasseh “made war with the Hagarites, with Jetur, and Nephish, and Nodab” (1 Chronicles 5:19). The sons of the son God did not choose became nations, exactly as He said.

corruption_summary: God's promises to the unchosen line are overlooked; Genesis records twelve Ishmaelite princes by name because God had said there would be twelve.
corruption_paragraphs: Election is sometimes preached as though God had no dealings at all with those outside the covenant line. Genesis 25 says otherwise. Ishmael is not the son of promise, and Ishmael is blessed, multiplied, and made a great nation with twelve named princes, because God had sworn it to Abraham for his sake.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the distinction between God's covenant mercy and His common goodness, both of which are real and neither of which is the other. Isaac inherited the covenant; Ishmael inherited a kingdom and a desert and twelve sons, and “they dwelt from Havilah unto Shur, that is before Egypt, as thou goest toward Assyria” (Genesis 25:18).

pos: n. (the twelfth and last son of Ishmael)
etymology: Hebrew Qedemah, eastward, or toward the east, from qedem, the east, the front, or ancient time; named at Genesis 25:15 and 1 Chronicles 1:31.
biblical_def: Kedemah closes the list of Ishmael's sons: “Hadar, and Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah” (Genesis 25:15); “Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael” (1 Chronicles 1:31). His name means eastward, and it describes where the whole family went. Abraham had sent the sons of his concubines “eastward, unto the east country” (Genesis 25:6), away from Isaac, and Ishmael's people settled on the desert frontier — “And they dwelt from Havilah unto Shur, that is before Egypt, as thou goest toward Assyria” (Genesis 25:18). The Hebrew word qedem carries two senses at once: the east, and what is ancient or in front. These were the peoples the Old Testament calls the children of the east, among whom Job lived and against whom Gideon rode. Kedemah is named once and then exists only as a direction on a map, which is in fact what his name says.

corruption_summary: Separation between the covenant line and the rest is read as tribal prejudice; Genesis presents it as God's own ordering, with provision made for both.
corruption_paragraphs: Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them eastward while he lived, and gave all that he had to Isaac. The arrangement looks harsh until the reason is stated: the covenant was with Isaac, and the covenant could not be divided among claimants. Provision was made; inheritance was not.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's electing purpose runs through one line without malice toward the others. Ishmael buried Abraham with Isaac at Machpelah, which the text records without comment. A son named eastward went east, and his descendants were still being named in Israel's books a thousand years later.

pos: n. (the sixth son of Joktan, of the line of Shem)
etymology: Hebrew Uzal, wandering, or a going forth, of uncertain root; named at Genesis 10:27 and 1 Chronicles 1:21.
biblical_def: Uzal belongs to the thirteen sons of Joktan in the table of nations: “And Hadoram, and Uzal, and Diklah” (Genesis 10:27), with the Chronicler's identical roll, “Hadoram also, and Uzal, and Diklah” (1 Chronicles 1:21). Joktan was of the line of Shem through Eber, and his sons are the peoples of southern Arabia: “And Joktan begat Almodad, and Sheleph, and Hazarmaveth, and Jerah” (Genesis 10:26). The chapter closes their account with a geography: “And their dwelling was from Mesha, as thou goest unto Sephar a mount of the east” (Genesis 10:30). Uzal is traditionally identified with the old name of the city that became Sana in the Yemen. These are the Semitic peoples who did not come into the covenant — Shem's line, but not Abraham's. The table of nations names them all, and says nothing further about most of them, because its business is to show that the whole earth is peopled from the three sons of Noah.

corruption_summary: The nations of Genesis 10 are treated as legendary ethnography; the chapter is the Bible's account of how a single family became the peoples of the earth.
corruption_paragraphs: Seventy nations are named in Genesis 10 and most receive no further mention anywhere. The modern habit is to treat the list as folk memory. But the chapter is doing precise work: it accounts for the whole known world from three men, it places each people geographically, and it sets up chapter 11, where those peoples are scattered from Babel, and chapter 12, where God calls one man out of them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that history has one origin and one Author, and that the Bible's account of the nations is history and not myth. Uzal is a name on that map, in the line of Shem, outside the covenant, in a chapter written so that no people on earth could think itself unaccounted for.

pos: n. (a son of Beriah, grandson of Asher, and father of Birzavith)
etymology: Hebrew Malki'el, God is my king, from melek, a king, with El, God; named at Genesis 46:17, Numbers 26:45 and 1 Chronicles 7:31.
biblical_def: Malchiel is one of the two sons of Beriah in the house of Asher: “And the sons of Asher; Jimnah, and Ishuah, and Isui, and Beriah, and Serah their sister: and the sons of Beriah; Heber, and Malchiel” (Genesis 46:17). He appears again as a clan in the wilderness census, “Of the sons of Beriah: of Heber, the family of the Heberites: of Malchiel, the family of the Malchielites” (Numbers 26:45), and once more with a detail added: “And the sons of Beriah; Heber, and Malchiel, who is the father of Birzavith” (1 Chronicles 7:31). He is named in Egypt, in the wilderness, and in Chronicles after the exile — three widely separated documents keeping the same household in view across a thousand years. His name is a confession: God is my king. It was borne by a man who went down into Egypt in Jacob's company, whose descendants came out under Moses, and whose family is still being reckoned by the Chronicler for a people under Persian rule.

corruption_summary: The kingship of God is treated as a metaphor for personal conviction; Israelite parents put it in their children's names as a statement about who actually rules.
corruption_paragraphs: To say God is my king now sounds like a declaration of private allegiance, one commitment among the many a person might hold. In Israel it was a claim about the constitution of the nation. Gideon refused a crown on that ground; Samuel treated the demand for a king as a rejection of the LORD; and the name Malchiel states the same thing in two words.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the actual, governing kingship of God over His people and over all nations. The name went down into Egypt with Jacob's household, passed through four hundred years of slavery, and was still being written in the registers after the exile, which is the sort of persistence a confession has when it is true.

pos: n. (a son of Heber, of the house of Asher)
etymology: Hebrew Yaphlet, he will deliver, or may he deliver, from palat, to escape or deliver; named twice, 1 Chronicles 7:32 and 7:33.
biblical_def: Japhlet is a grandson of Beriah in Asher's line: “And Heber begat Japhlet, and Shomer, and Hotham, and Shua their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:32), and his own sons follow immediately: “And the sons of Japhlet; Pasach, and Bimhal, and Ashvath. These are the children of Japhlet” (1 Chronicles 7:33). He is not to be confused with Japhleti, the border-clan on Ephraim's frontier in Joshua 16:3, which is a different name in a different tribe. Asher's genealogy is brief but it is given in full depth for a few households, and this is one of them: Beriah, Heber, Japhlet, and Japhlet's three sons. The summary of the whole tribe follows a few verses later: these were “heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes” (1 Chronicles 7:40). His name means he will deliver, one of the commonest confessions in Hebrew naming, built on the same root as Palti, Peletiah and Elpalet.

corruption_summary: Similar names are merged for convenience; Japhlet of Asher and the Japhleti of Ephraim's border are different, and Scripture keeps them apart.
corruption_paragraphs: The Hebrew Bible has many names that differ by a letter, and the careless habit is to treat near-identical forms as one. Japhlet is a man of Asher in 1 Chronicles 7; Japhleti is a border coast in the inheritance of Ephraim in Joshua 16. Different tribe, different kind of thing, different text. A reference work that conflates them has misreported two passages at once.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that precision in reading is owed to a God who inspired the particulars. The name itself is the common Hebrew prayer for rescue, and it is the whole of what we know about the man — that and three sons and a father.

pos: n. (a coast or border clan on the southern frontier of Ephraim's inheritance)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Yaphleti, the Japhletite, from the same root as Japhlet, palat, to deliver; named once, Joshua 16:3.
biblical_def: Japhleti is a boundary marker, not a man. The southern border of Joseph's inheritance is traced: “And goeth down westward to the coast of Japhleti, unto the coast of Bethhoron the nether, and to Gezer: and the goings out thereof are at the sea” (Joshua 16:3). The clan is otherwise unknown, and it is not the family of Japhlet the Asherite, who belonged to a different tribe in a different part of the land. The surrounding verses give Ephraim's frontier in detail — Ataroth-addar, Beth-horon the upper, Beth-horon the nether, Gezer, the sea — and the whole chapter is part of the most carefully surveyed section of the Old Testament. Joshua 13 to 21 fixes the inheritance of every tribe town by town and landmark by landmark, so that there could be no later dispute. A clan nobody can now identify was a known landmark then, and the LORD had the surveyors write it down.

corruption_summary: Detailed boundary lists are skipped as tedious; they are the legal instrument by which God prevented the strong tribes from devouring the weak.
corruption_paragraphs: Nine chapters of landmarks is the longest stretch of apparently unreadable material in the historical books. Its function is plain enough once stated: a written, witnessed, divinely-authorised survey is what stands between a small clan and a powerful neighbour. Every ridge and spring and ruined town named in Joshua 16 is a fence post.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God defends the weak by law and by record, not merely by sentiment. “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Proverbs 22:28) presupposes that the landmark was set, recorded and known. Japhleti is one of them, and we no longer know where it was, which is why it had to be written down at the time.

pos: n. (a son of Ephraim, head of the family of the Tahanites; also a name in the Ephraimite descent of Joshua)
etymology: Hebrew Tachan, encampment, or graciousness, from chanah, to encamp or pitch a tent; named at Numbers 26:35 and 1 Chronicles 7:25.
biblical_def: Tahan is an Ephraimite family head in the wilderness census: “These are the sons of Ephraim after their families: of Shuthelah, the family of the Shuthalhites: of Becher, the family of the Bachrites: of Tahan, the family of the Tahanites” (Numbers 26:35). The name occurs again in the Chronicler's descent of the same tribe: “And Rephah was his son, also Resheph, and Telah his son, and Tahan his son” (1 Chronicles 7:25), a line that runs down through Laadan, Ammihud, Elishama, Nun, and so to Joshua. The chapter also preserves the only mention in Scripture of a woman who built cities: “And his daughter was Sherah, who built Bethhoron the nether, and the upper, and Uzzensherah” (1 Chronicles 7:24). Tahan's name is from the root for pitching a tent, which is what his family did for forty years before any of them built anything.

corruption_summary: Forty years of tents is read as wasted time; Scripture treats the wilderness as the place where a people learned to live at God's word and move at His cloud.
corruption_paragraphs: The generation that died in the wilderness is remembered chiefly for its unbelief, and rightly. But the generation that grew up there learned something no settled people learns: to pitch and to strike camp at the moving of a cloud, to eat bread that came daily, and to carry a tabernacle rather than build a temple.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God trains His people in conditions they would not choose. A family named encampment belonged to the tribe of Ephraim, and the line that passed through it produced Joshua, who led Israel out of the tents and into the land.

pos: n. (a son in the Ephraimite line that runs down to Joshua)
etymology: Hebrew Rephach, riches, or support, of uncertain root, possibly kin to rapha, to heal; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:25.
biblical_def: Rephah stands at the head of a short Ephraimite descent: “And Rephah was his son, also Resheph, and Telah his son, and Tahan his son” (1 Chronicles 7:25). The verses before it carry one of the saddest episodes in the genealogies — the sons of Ephraim slain by the men of Gath “because they came down to take away their cattle” (1 Chronicles 7:21), and Ephraim mourning many days while his brethren came to comfort him, and then a son born and named Beriah, “because it went evil with his house” (1 Chronicles 7:23). Out of that grief the line continues: a daughter who built three cities, and then Rephah, Resheph, Telah, Tahan, Laadan, Ammihud, Elishama, Non, Jehoshuah. The last of those is Joshua the son of Nun. A household that had buried its sons to cattle-raiders is the household from which the conqueror of Canaan came.

corruption_paragraphs: Ephraim's sons were killed in a cattle raid, and the text says he mourned many days and his brethren came to comfort him. That is as near as the genealogies come to narrative, and it is left there without resolution. Then the list resumes, and eight generations later it arrives at the man who divided the land.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's purposes are not interrupted by the griefs He permits. The son born after the loss was named Beriah, because it went evil with his house, and Beriah's line produced Joshua. Nothing in Scripture suggests the mourning was less than real; everything in the genealogy says it was not final.

pos: n. (a son in the Ephraimite line that runs down to Joshua)
etymology: Hebrew Resheph, a flame, a burning coal, or a lightning-bolt, from a root signifying to burn; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:25.
biblical_def: Resheph is named beside Rephah: “And Rephah was his son, also Resheph, and Telah his son, and Tahan his son” (1 Chronicles 7:25). The Hebrew word resheph is a common noun elsewhere in Scripture, meaning a flame or a burning bolt — it is the word in the Song of Solomon, “the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame” (Song 8:6), and in Habakkuk, “burning coals went forth at his feet” (Habakkuk 3:5). In the nations round about, Resheph was also the name of a god of plague and lightning, which makes its use as an Israelite personal name worth noticing: the Hebrews took the word back as a word. The line it stands in is the Ephraimite descent that reaches Joshua, and it comes immediately after the house of Ephraim had been struck by grief and had begun again.

corruption_summary: Shared vocabulary with pagan religion is read as borrowing; Israel used the common words of its neighbours while denying every claim those neighbours made with them.
corruption_paragraphs: The peoples around Israel had a god called Resheph, lord of plague and the lightning stroke. Scripture uses the same word as a plain noun for flame and as a man's name, with no trace of the deity attached. The habit is consistent: Israel used the word for the sun, the word for the sea, the word for dawn, all of them divine names elsewhere, and all of them creatures in Hebrew.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the God of Scripture owns the vocabulary, because He owns the things it names. “Before him went the pestilence, and burning coals went forth at his feet” (Habakkuk 3:5). What the nations worshipped, the prophets described as the servants that run before the LORD.

pos: n. (the first-named son of Becher, of the tribe of Benjamin)
etymology: Hebrew Zemirah, a song, or melody, from zamar, to sing or make music; named once, 1 Chronicles 7:8.
biblical_def: Zemira heads the list of Becher's nine sons: “And the sons of Becher; Zemira, and Joash, and Eliezer, and Elioenai, and Omri, and Jerimoth, and Abiah, and Anathoth, and Alameth. All these are the sons of Becher” (1 Chronicles 7:8). Benjamin's register in this chapter closes with a muster: “And the number of them, after their genealogy by their generations, heads of the house of their fathers, mighty men of valour, was twenty thousand and two hundred” (1 Chronicles 7:9). His name is the Hebrew word for a song. It is the root behind mizmor, the word standing at the head of fifty-seven psalms and translated in the titles as Psalm; behind the Levitical singers; behind the command to sing praises. Two of his brothers, Anathoth and Alameth, gave their names to towns of Benjamin — Anathoth being the birthplace of Jeremiah. A tribe counted for war names its sons after a melody.

corruption_summary: Music is treated as decoration around the real business of religion; in Israel it was a Levitical office, a standing command, and a name parents gave their sons.
corruption_paragraphs: Song is easily demoted to an accompaniment of worship rather than part of it. Scripture gives it an establishment: courses of singers appointed by David, instruments specified, psalms written to be sung, and the whole congregation commanded. “Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving, and make a joyful noise unto him with psalms” (Psalm 95:2) uses the very root of this man's name.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that praise is commanded worship, not optional atmosphere, and that the church sings because God has told it to. A warrior tribe of twenty thousand two hundred mighty men of valour had a household head named Song.
